narrative:
The model determined that you have a 96.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students likely to pass, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the greatest influence. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) was far below the average of roughly 6 among accepted students and strongly pushed the model toward predicting failure. Your LSAT score of 26 was the second most important factor; it sits well below the 37-point average of accepted students and added further weight toward a negative outcome. Finally, your first-year class ranking in the lowest decile (again 1 versus an average near 6) also pulled the prediction in the same direction, though less forcefully than the other two.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your solid undergraduate GPA of 3.3, middle-income background, and plan to attend full-time. Gender and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and test scores in a future application would likely shift the prediction enough to make admission possible. Consider targeted test preparation or additional coursework before reapplying.
